background.definition: SCI is compression, contusion, and/or partial or complete transection of the spinal cord. This section focuses on traumatic injury, rather than malignancy, hematoma, or infectious processes.

list.listitem: 12,000 new cases of SCI each year.
More common in men, young adults and adolescents.
Over 255,000 affected by SCI living in the US.
Loss in wages, fringe benefits and productivity averages $62,270 per person per year, or $16 billion/year nationwide.
Average cost of care for tetraplegics is $500,000 to $775,000 in the first year, and $57,000 to $139,000 for each following year.
Trauma (motor vehicle accidents, diving accidents, sports injuries, penetrating trauma)
Intervertebral disc herniation
Atraumatic vertebral fracture (compression) with displacement of bony fragment(s)
Primary injury is structural damage to the cord occurring with the trauma, or after moving an unstabilized injured spine.
Secondary injury is caused by ischemia, hypoxia, edema, and biochemical events shortly after the injury. These are usually caused by unrelieved compression of the cord.
Patients with neurologic deficits corresponding to a dermatome "level" following trauma must have spinal column and/or spinal cord imaging to evaluate for SCI. C
Differentiation between complete and incomplete injuries, as well as the various cord syndromes (anterior, posterior, etc) is essential to guide further management. C
Midline cervical tenderness is the most reliable cervical spine injury sign. B
Validated clinical rules such as NEXUS and the Canadian C-spine rules exist to guide imaging. A

Differential.Differential_Features: Paresis of arms greater than legs
Paralysis and hyperesthesia at level of injury, intact light touch and vibration
Impaired light touch and proprioception at level of injury
Ipsilateral motor and proprioception loss, contralateral pain and temperature loss
Any voluntary movement or preserved sensation below the level of injury
Lack of physiological disturbances such as bradycardia, hypotension, etc

list.listitem: Obtain a history of the mechanism of injury from the patient and from witnesses, if possible. Any impaired trauma patient needs C-spine evaluation, even in the absence of neurologic signs and symptoms.
Perform a detailed neurologic examination to define level and completeness of injury (see ASIA system, ).
Do not remove protective equipment, ie, football helmets or pads when a potential injury has occurred unless airway cannot otherwise be managed.

Midline neck tenderness is most reliable single finding to rule in cervical spine fracture. Absence of midline neck tenderness, intoxication, altered level of consciousness, and severe pain make cervical spine injury unlikely.

In a retrospective study of 278 adults evaluated in EDs for near-shore aquatic head and spinal injuries, midline spine tenderness was associated with thoracic (LR+ 2.6) and lumbar (LR+ 3.5) spinal fractures, while paralysis (LR +13.9), sensory loss (LR+ 5.8), and diffuse weakness (LR + 5.3) were associated with spinal cord injuries.
Being up and about at the scene, direct blow to neck, neck pain, tenderness over posterolateral neck muscles, and soft tissue injury are not helpful individually for diagnosing SCI.
The initial laboratory assessment should include ABG, CBC, chemistry panel, coagulation profile, cardiac enzyme profile, urinalysis, toxicology screen, CXR, and ECG.

Order imaging of the spine (plain films, CT) and/or spinal cord (MRI). CT scan is extremely helpful for bony injury, particularly when the C-spine cannot be "cleared" with plain films due to immobilization or body habitus. MRI is required to directly visualize of the spinal cord, and is indicated for SCI without radiographic abnormality (SCIWORA).
The NEXUS () or Canadian C-spine rule are helpful in deciding if C-spine radiography is indicated.

A study compared assessment of the Canadian C-spine rule in the field by paramedics with physician investigators. Paramedics had 91% sensitivity and 67% specificity, and the kappa for interrater agreement was 0.94 which is excellent. No misclassifications were judged to have caused harm.
Evaluate any trauma patient who has impaired ability to give a history for C-spine injury. Stabilize trauma patients with neurologic deficits while en route to a diagnostic facility.

Other life-threatening injuries must be managed per Advanced Trauma Life Support guidelines. Hypotension, bradycardia, and respiratory insufficiency often accompany cord injuries. Spine stabilization en route to hospital.
Spine imaging appropriate to level(s) of neurologic injury follows stabilization of cardiorespiratory status. In 15% of cases, there are multiple fractures.
Perform a detailed neurologic evaluation (see ASIA system, ).
Immobilize spine during transport to hospital. C
Early surgical intervention is indicated for selected patients with neurological deterioration and if incomplete SCI with persistent spinal cord deformity. B
Whenever possible, compression hose or pneumatic devices should be applied to the legs of all patients for the first 2 weeks following injury. C
If patient meets standard diagnostic criteria for depression following SCI, select appropriate antidepressant medications. C
Routine use of methylprednisolone for acute SCI cannot be recommended. B

Two clinical trials (National Adult Social Care Intelligence Service II and III) and a Cochrane review both support a clinical benefit of high-dose methylprednisolone given within 8 hours of injury.However, review and reanalysis of the data has found that steroids are associated with longer hospital stay and higher acute care charges (mostly due to infectious complications). The small statistical difference in function is of uncertain clinical relevance. Current guidelines therefore only recommend their use in the context of an informed discussion with patients of the risks and possible benefits.
Avoid hypotension and maintain DBP in the 85 to 90 range for 7 days after injury.
Initiate thromboprophylaxis with either low molecular weight heparin or adjusted dose unfractionated heparin within 72 hours after SCI, provided there is no active bleeding or coagulopathy.
Gabapentin relieves neuropathic pain in paraplegia after spine injury. Give 900 mg/day for the first week, 1800mg/day in week 2, 2400 mg/day in week 3, then 3600 mg/day in week 4.
Amitriptyline at 50 mg TID maintenance dose relieves neuropathic pain in SCI in people who have considerable depressive symptomatology.
Carbamazepine decreased neuropathic pain after SCI at 1-month but not at 3- or 6-month followup.
Sildenafil is effective in the treatment of erectile dysfunction among men with SCI.
Intrathecal baclofen is helpful in reducing spasticity for patients with incomplete cord lesions.
There is no evidence from two RCTs that gangliosides improve any clinical outcomes.
For patients with outlet constipation, a small pilot RCT with 16 patients found that botulinum toxin type A infiltration of the external anal sphincter provided some improvement in symptoms.
An observational study found an association between earlier initiation of anticoagulation following injury (the median was 65 hours) and a lower likelihood of venous thromboembolism.
Surgery may be used to perform decompression laminectomy, to remove bone and other tissue fragments, and to fuse fractured bones.

A variety of novel treatments are being studied, such as spinal cord stimulation. The latter was initial used as part of a pain management program but is now being studied for its ability to improve volitional muscle function.
Stem cell therapies have not been conclusively shown to be beneficial and safe in humans with SCI.
Non-invasive electical stimulation may be effective for patients with spasticity.
Self-administered bladder neuromodulation reduced the need for overactive bladder medications in an RCT.
Isolated cervical spine fractures are associated with an unfavorable outcome in the elderly population regardless of associated traumatic injuries or SCI. C
Selected patients with complete injuries can reasonably hope for one or two levels of improvement at one year after the injury. Recovery plateaus at 6 to 12 months after injury. C
In the absence of immediate immobilization and early stabilization of fractures, outlook is bleak.
The importance of discriminating between partial and complete spinal cord lesions is critical in order to determine prognosis.
Isolated cervical spine fractures are associated with an unfavorable outcome in the elderly population regardless of associated traumatic injuries or SCI.
Selected patients with complete injuries can reasonably hope for one or two levels of improvement at one year after the injury. Recovery plateaus at 6 to 12 months after injury.
Patients with short interval to release of cord compression and younger patients have better outcomes.
A clinical prediction rule developed and validated at 19 European centers between 2001 and 2008 predicts ambulation outcomes after traumatic SCI.
Careful follow-up with attention to respiratory status, bladder function, and skin care are essential.
Rehabilitation should focus on assistive devices, bowel and bladder regimens, and vocational opportunities.
Depression is common, and patients should be screened at least annually.
Children have disproportionately high frequencies of upper C-spine injury, SCIWORA, complete neurological injuries, and delayed onset of neurological deficits.

feature.feature_body: If a patient has any of the following, order cervical spine radiography: Posterior midline cervical spine tenderness Evidence of intoxication Abnormal level of alertness Any focal neurologic deficit Any painful distracting injuries
